17129-the-missing-link:
Edward Dyson's 1922 novel centers on Nicholas Crips, called Nickie the Kid, a smooth talker who lives by wits on the edge of honest work and crime. His healing mixture opens the tale, and his circle of beats, sharpers, and soft marks gives the book its comic edge. Dyson paints Crips as bony, pale, and quick with a tale of sickness when a tale pays.

The humor comes from cons, near misses, and the gap between Crips' fine talk and his thin deeds. Set in Australian low life of its day, the novel mixes slang, satire, and caper plot. Readers who like rogues with charm and no shame will enjoy watching Nickie talk his way in and out of trouble.
21015-the-adventures-of-jimmy-skunk:
Peter Rabbit watches Jimmy Skunk vanish into an old barrel on a hill in Thornton Burgess's tale. The Imp of Mischief whispers at once in Peter's long ears, Burgess warns. Jimmy, once started, will not keep still unless made to, all agree.

The Adventures of Jimmy Skunk, from 1918, joins Burgess's vast bedtime story world. Reddy Fox, Peter Rabbit, and the Green Forest crew fill its small wars. Each scrape teaches real skunk lore beneath the fun and talk. Burgess wrote to make children love wild neighbours, and Jimmy's calm, smelly defence still wins that case.
21412-the-tale-of-bobby-bobolink:
Bobby Bobolink arrives in Pleasant Valley in Arthur Scott Bailey's Tale of Bobby Bobolink, a 1920 Sleepy-Time Tale. On May Day the feathered folk stop, look, and listen for the friend all await. Bobby is a singing bird of the meadows, proud of his song.

Chapters follow his greetings, his singing for a mate, and the house in the meadow. Johnnie Green, the farmer's boy, breaks in more than once, and Bobby must fool him. Mr Crow, Mr Catbird, and Timothy Turtle add fun and friction. Bailey's short tales give young readers a whole small world of field and swamp folk.
21845-the-tale-of-peter-mink:
Peter Mink has no home and a very long neck, and both facts shape this 1916 children's tale by Arthur Scott Bailey. Peter has no home because he does not want one; he sleeps wherever he happens to find a snug place. His clothes wear out fast from squeezing through small holes and cracks. In Pleasant Valley, everyone knows his shifting ways.

The chapters set Peter to sawing wood, passing the hat, and helping Jimmy Rabbit, whom he pulls out of the mud. A garden party, a circus parade, and a duck pond fill out his adventures. Bailey writes animal life as village comedy for young readers. Peter's bad temper and good turns make him a full little character in fur.
22876-the-link:
A starship slides toward its berth in The Link, a piece of science fiction. Other vessels tower around the berth in ring after ring, their bright spires aimed at the sky. Then the view blots out as grapples pull the vessel into the slot from which it rose days before.

Arrival is only the start. Stories named for a link usually promise a connection that changes everything, between worlds, minds, or times. This one builds its future from harbor routine in space, ships handled like liners at a dock. The method keeps the strange scene credible. Readers of classic magazine science fiction will recognize the manner, economical, visual, and more interested in the working future than in speeches about it.
23210-missing-link:
Missing Link is a work of science fiction set aboard a starship. Its central figure is a heavy planet native who feels uneasy on Gienah III. That world's gravity runs at only seven-eighths of Earth's standard, and the difference nags at him as he works.

On the bridge, he checks the control console, the chronometer, and a big glowing map of their position. Surgical scars on his neck, where tiny communications gear was set in, itch badly. The tale builds its future from such details: altered bodies, ship routine, and a man far from the heavy world that made him.
24005-but-i-don-t-think:
Randall Garrett's But, I Don't Think opens with a quotation from The Idle Worshipers by R. Phillip Dachboden. A physician, a painter, and a philosopher debate a religion with human sacrifice as an integral part, and the philosopher asks, with irritation, whether the victim might like it that way.

The story proper begins as the great merchantship Naipor settles tens of thousands of tons into her landing cradle on Viornis, gently as an egg into an egg crate. Space Captain Humbolt Reed orders High Lieutenant Blyke to bring the Guesser to his office at once. Garrett's tale is a spacefaring argument about freedom, slavery, and what thinking men think they know.
24246-greener-than-you-think:
Ward Moore wrote this novel, published by William Sloane Associates in New York in 1947, in a first edition. Its chapters run from Albert Weener Begins and Consequences of a Discovery through Man Triumphant in two parts, a South Pacific sailing discovery, and Mr. Weener Sees It Through. A note warns that neither the vegetation nor the people are entirely fictitious, yet no person pictured is the reader.

With one exception, Moore adds: the reader, whatever the country or station, is Albert Weener, as Moore himself is Albert Weener. The narrator once dreamed of writing a book to ease weary minds of the day's cares. Readers get a wry, unsettling tale of an ordinary man and a discovery that grows beyond him.
25095-joe-strong-the-boy-fish-or-marvelo:
Vance Barnum's Joe Strong, the Boy Fish, subtitled Marvelous Doings in a Big Tank, is a boys' circus adventure from the Whitman series about the young performer Joe Strong. The story opens at a packed circus, with bands playing, elephants trumpeting, and Joe preparing his acrobatic and trapeze turns.

Trouble follows quickly: a savage lion escapes its cage, and Joe must help keep the show going while the beast is loose near the grounds. A water act with a dog named Toto adds to the excitement. The book delivers exactly what its title promises, fast action, circus color, and a hero who keeps his nerve.
25523-old-junk:
H. M. Tomlinson selects travel and chance stories from his writings in periodicals between January 1907 and April 1918, arranged in order of time. He dedicates the book to C. H. G. H., a companion on much of what it describes, killed in action in Artois in August 1918.

Chapters run from the African coast and the call of the sea through old junk, bed-books and night-lights, the pit mouth, and the voyage of the Mona. Tomlinson writes as a watcher and wanderer, finding meaning in derelicts, lascars, and extra hands aboard ship.
2648-george-cruikshank:
William Makepeace Thackeray wrote this essay on George Cruikshank, reprinted from the Westminster Review of June 1840. Thackeray opens on ingratitude, a charge laid against every inhabitant of a wicked world, and on men borne through trouble like swimmers in a crowd.

Cruikshank's etchings, crowded with rogues, dandies, and drunkards, get a critic who loves their energy and moral bite. Thackeray judges the artist as a historian of low life and high folly alike. The essay remains a lively tribute, and a reminder of how much Victorian England learned about itself from pictures.
27425-major-frank:
A. L. G. Bosboom-Toussaint wrote this Dutch novel, translated by James Akeroyd and published by T. Fisher Unwin in London in 1885. It opens with a letter from Sir Leopold van Zonshoven at The Hague in March 1865 to his friend William Verheyst, begging him to come at once, since something wonderful has happened.

Leopold, a poor gentleman who has barely kept out of debt by strict economy, has all at once come into an immense fortune. His mother's old aunt, unknown to him and quarrelled with all her relations, made him sole heir to all her property. A million, he writes, has been thrown at his head. The novel that follows turns on fortune, friendship, and its surprises.
28871-the-seven-great-monarchies-of-the-:
David Widger edited this linked index to George Rawlinson's Seven Great Monarchies of the Ancient Asian World, with his History of Phoenicia. Rawlinson, who lived from 1812 to 1902, treats Chaldaea, Assyria, Media, Babylon, Persia, Parthia, and the Sassanian Empire. Each monarchy gets chapters on country, climate, people, language, arts, manners, religion, and history.

The Chaldaea section alone lists plates of Mugheir ruins, Warka, cuneiform inscriptions, and a restored temple. The index lets a reader move through Rawlinson's vast survey monarchy by monarchy, with pictures and plans beside the text. Scholars and general readers get a guide to a classic Victorian history of the ancient Near East, still useful for its scope and illustrations.
29698-lighter-than-you-think:
Nelson Bond's short tale of Pat Pending, the greatest inventulator of all time, comes from Blue Book, which printed more than a dozen Pat Pending stories. Sandy beams at everyone, her eyes needing only jet propulsion to become flying saucers. Was Pat not wonderful? A joker of old won two-bit immortality by saying the nation wants a cheap cigar.

Bond answers with Victorian malarkey: the nation really wants a cheap nickel, or a cigar-shaped spaceship. A fortune waits among the stars for whoever can travel lighter than he thinks. Fans of Bond will enjoy a light, laughing tale of invention, with a federal employee of the Patent Office at its heart.
33606-the-fairy-school-of-castle-frank:
Grant Balfour writes a Canadian fairy tale for children in this 1899 Toronto book, recommended by Ontario's premier, G. W. Ross, as interesting, instructive, and morally useful. One hundred years before the telling, a boy named Robin lived in the grand old Canadian woods among wapitis, wolves, and bears. His wooden home was called Castle Frank, near a deep ravine and a slow river flowing into a great blue lake.

Eight chapters follow Romantic Robin into fairyland, a strange school class, advice from Hug-grippy the affectionate and from a subtle snake, a modest medallist, a fight in the ravine, and Robin's book. Balfour mixes woodland adventure with lessons in courage and kindness. Young readers will enjoy its Canadian setting and its gentle fairy-school fantasy.
8430-the-mountebank:
William J. Locke's novel opens in June 1919, when the narrator receives a long letter from Brigadier-General Andrew Lackaday, sent from an obscure hotel in Marseilles, with a bulky manuscript. Lackaday kept his friend up till morning with his story, and the manuscript that follows tells it: the life of a mountebank, a showman and wanderer, in Locke's warm, romantic style.

Locke, a popular novelist of the Edwardian years, writes of outsiders with sympathy, and Lackaday's tale moves between war, show business, and love. Readers get a framed narrative, a letter opening a life, in the tradition of stories told by friends. The novel's charm lies in its hero, a performer who lives by his wits and his heart.
9462-the-tale-of-sandy-chipmunk:
Arthur Scott Bailey wrote The Tale of Sandy Chipmunk in 1916, a children's animal tale from his Sleepy-Time series. Sandy, a young chipmunk, gets his name, builds a house, and learns the ways of field and farm. Harry L. Smith drew the pictures, which show Sandy's mishaps in bright scenes. The book speaks in short, plain words for small readers.

Chapters follow a broken egg, samples of wheat, a store kept by Uncle Sammy, and work for Mr. Crow. Sandy gets a letter, rides to the miller's, and plants corn in his turn. A reader gets a gentle woodland tale of work, friends, and growing up, told with humor and a fond eye for small beasts.
949-tom-swift-and-his-submarine-boat-or-:
Tom Swift builds a submarine boat in this adventure by Victor Appleton, and he sails under the ocean for sunken treasure. News of a treasure wreck starts the tale, and Mr. Berg, a rival, grows astonished, then suspicious, as Tom finishes his craft. Tom is even imprisoned before he turns the tables.

Mr. Damon joins the voyage, Captain Weston aids the search, and the sea yields perils and prizes in turn. Appleton writes with brisk, boyish energy, mixing invention with adventure. The book is a classic Tom Swift tale, where a young inventor's machine opens a hidden world beneath the waves.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-paula-v:
Franz Paula von Schrank, born at Varnbach near Scharding on the Inn on 21 August 1747 and died at Munich on 22 December 1835, was a German Jesuit naturalist and botanist.

After the suppression he was ordained priest at Vienna in December 1774, took a theology doctorate in 1776, and published his first natural history contributions. He taught mathematics and physics at Amberg and rhetoric at Burghausen, studying agriculture there, and in 1784 became professor of agriculture, mining, forestry, botany, and zoology at Ingolstadt University, later Landshut. In 1809 the Munich Academy made him director of its new botanical garden, his life's work thereafter. His writings fill nine columns in the Jesuit bibliography, closing with scriptural works on the six days of creation and a literal commentary on Genesis.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-xaver-v:
Franz Xaver von Funk, born at Abtsgmund in Wurttemberg on 12 October 1840 and died at Tubingen on 24 February 1907, was a German church historian whose critical method founded a school. Son of an innkeeper, he attended Ellwangen gymnasium and entered Tubingen University in 1859. He lived at the Wilhelmsstift, studied philosophy and theology with ancient philology and political economy. He won the political science faculty prize of 1862 for an essay on what police meant in the eighteenth century.

 Back in 1866, he became tutor at the Wilhelmsstift, guiding students' personal studies. He rose to Tubingen's church history chair, where his sole aim, seeking historical truth, frank and honest character, and severity toward opponents swayed by other motives created a school. It advanced earnest, scholarly criticism among German Catholic historians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michael-sigis:
Michael Sigismund Frank, a Catholic artist and rediscoverer of the lost art of glass painting, was born at Nuremberg on 1 June 1770 and died at Munich on 16 January 1847. His father, a well-off provisions dealer, meant him for the business, but the boy's passion for art thwarted the plan. His mother, unknown to her husband, had him taught drawing at the local academy, where his progress astonished friends.

Orphaned young, Frank was apprenticed to his godfather Neubert, who lacquered and decorated wooden boxes and caskets at Nuremberg. Back with his remarried mother, he studied drawing again, painting boxes for other makers to pay his way. At twenty-one his parents pressed him, against his will, to wed Marie Blechkoll, whose dowry brought the inn Zur Himmelsleiter. Frank was no innkeeper: while his wife ran the hotel, he kept studying art and turned to porcelain painting.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monk:
A monk is a man living in community apart from the world. He lives under vows of poverty, chastity and obedience, following the rule of his particular order. The word itself is popular rather than official church language. Its English form comes through Anglo-Saxon munuc from Latin monachus, a borrowing of Greek monachos. That Greek root ties to ideas of solitude and unity.

Early church fathers already disagreed about the root. Jerome stressed the solitary, while Augustine stressed the oneness of brethren living as one. The entry traces the word's history. It separates monks proper from friars and canons. It notes how the solitary hermit gave way to community life under a rule, with the great orders of East and West shaping what monkhood became.
doe-osti-2589593-probabilistic-error-bou: Tensor decompositions got their error bounds, and this DOE LDRD report covers the probabilistic analysis. The pages detail the large-scale methods. The data scientists get their numbers. The report was LDRD. The applications were data analysis. The scientists got numbers.
doe-osti-3021931-evaluation-of-hanford-2: Hanford tanks got physically evaluated, and this DOE text studies 200 West farms. The pages detail the property findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The farms were tank. The data were nuclear. The West was 200. The data were physical. The farms were 241-S.
george-cruikshank:
William Makepeace Thackeray praised the caricaturist George Cruikshank in this essay from the Westminster Review of June 1840. Thackeray opens with a meditation on ingratitude, lost youth, and the fog of adult striving, then turns to the artist whose drawings had delighted that youth. Cruikshank illustrated fairy tales, Dickens, and the drunkard's progress of popular prints, and Thackeray knew the work as a fellow pen-and-pencil man.

The essay mixes memoir, criticism, and gratitude, urging a busy world to honor the humorist who stocked its imagination. Thackeray writes of Cruikshank's grotesques, his temperance plates, and his fairy grotesquerie with a cartoonist's professional love. It is one Victorian artist's tribute to another, and a small classic of appreciative criticism.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIATerpilFrank_:
Frank Terpil had been a CIA contract man before he became an international arms dealer, and the Washington Post's Arms Agent With Hazardous Habit catches him at the fall. Terpil was arrested for trying to sell 10,000 machine guns to men who turned out to be undercover detectives.

Together with Edwin Wilson, Terpil became the emblem of the ex-agent gone rogue: agency training and contacts turned to private gunrunning for dictators and middlemen. His later flight from American justice completed the legend. The article is preserved as the newspaper's account of the arrest that started his downfall.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DonnerFrank_Don:
The December 1, 1984 issue of The Nation magazine carries an article by Harrison E. Salisbury with an unlikely subject. Its title is The Strange Correspondence of Morris Ernst and John Edgar Hoover, 1939-1964. Ernst was a famed civil liberties lawyer; Hoover ran the FBI. Their letters ran for twenty-five years.

Salisbury's piece examines what passed between a man who defended free speech and the director who kept files on dissenters. The friendship puzzled both men's reputations. The issue preserves the article as readers first met it, inside a leading journal of the American left.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WrightFrank_Wri: A letter dated June 30, 1968, went to Frank Wright of the Freedom Institute. The writer's name is not recorded in the record. Letters to small political and educational groups filled many research files of the period. The Wright letter is one surviving piece of that traffic, written while debate over the Warren Report and the King and Robert Kennedy killings was at full heat.
podcast-dannyjones-TAzeJl8n4nk:
Jimmy Corsetti, who researches ancient mysteries online, and Dan Richards join Danny Jones for a crowded hour. One subject is a new controversy over Gobekli Tepe's excavation and future. The other is the earth's next magnetic pole flip. The guests discuss the flip as a coming event with ancient precedents.

Corsetti has fought publicly with archaeologists over access and interpretation at the Turkish site, and he states that fight here. The pole flip thread adds geophysics to archaeology, two slow sciences asked to deliver sudden drama. The guests' readings are their own, contested by both fields they borrow from. The episode preserves the current state of alternative archaeology's two favorite live stories, argued by the men driving them, in the room where their audiences actually gather.
podcast-joerogan-QCJUEqppqNk:
Author Douglas Murray talks with Rogan, in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience, about people's need for religion. Murray, a British writer on culture and politics, argues that the hunger for the sacred does not die when churches empty. It moves somewhere else.

He traces where that hunger goes: into politics, identity, and new moral codes that act like faiths. Rogan asks whether anything can fill the gap without the old harms of dogma. The segment is a compact statement of Murray's case for the sacred, made in conversation rather than in print, and open to pushback.
podcast-joerogan-fds6Nm1QQNk:
Playwright David Mamet talks with Rogan, in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience, about the mythology of the Bible. Mamet, one of America's great dramatists, is also a sharp and cranky reader of scripture. His take honors the book's stories while refusing easy piety.

He argues that the Bible's tales carry the deep patterns of human life, which is why they still grip readers who share none of the faith. Rogan asks how a playwright reads characters like Abraham and Moses. The segment is a writer's tour of the good book, brisk, funny, and serious about story above all.
podcast-tuckercarlson-vUFtmvlOANk:
A journalist who lived in Israel for ten years joins Tucker Carlson to revisit October 7. Carlson says American news filters hide too much of the story. He calls the attack the start of a global shift.

The guest argues that a full timeline is needed to grasp that day. The title charges that Israel's leader funded Hamas for years. They discuss foreknowledge, dead Palestinians, and political gain. The talk is grave and detailed. It will draw listeners who want a critical account that American outlets rarely give in full. The claims are grave and fully aired.
the-missing-link:
Edward Dyson's 1922 novel The Missing Link opens with Dr. Crips's Healing Mixture, its first chapter. Nicholas Crips, called Nickie the Kid by his familiars, earns the nickname from kidder, a term for a smooth, flattering schemer with hidden motives. Even among companions expert in pretence, Nickie stood out as a specialist.

Crips is a thin, bony man of about five feet nine, often unshaven, whose worn black suit and moth-eaten cap suit his trade. Spareness helped him plead chronic sickness at back doors. When the chapter opens he is calling on housewives, retailing what hospital doctors supposedly said about his interesting heart weakness. His circle, the narrator explains, sat on the rail between honest work and open crime.
the-mountebank:
William J. Locke's novel The Mountebank begins in June 1919, when its narrator receives a long letter and a bulky manuscript from Brigadier-General Andrew Lackaday. The letter comes from an obscure hotel in Marseilles. Lackaday recounts how the narrator once listened all night to his wretched affairs and suggested he write a book about himself.

Lackaday protests that a layman cannot manage coherent narrative, and that English is nearly a foreign language to him, since he has thought all his life in French. Even the letter's prelude cost him two cigarettes. Instead he sends raw material from memory and diary: 673 sprawling foolscap pages covering his life, which, astonishingly, cut out the war years entirely, as the narrator marvels.
the-tale-of-sandy-chipmunk: Sandy Chipmunk, dated 1916, is one of Arthur Scott Bailey's Sleepy-Time Tales, illustrated by Harry L. Smith. Title page and contents are what this record offers, and Sandy's adventures stop before they start. Fourteen listed chapters cover a broken egg, house building, samples of wheat, a basket of corn, work for Mr. Crow, and a ride to the miller's. One picture caption shows Sandy so startled that he dropped the eggs. The outline promises a small, busy chipmunk learning farmyard lessons the hard way.
tom-swift-and-his-submarine-boat-or-unde:
Victor Appleton opens his submarine story with a rushing, throbbing noise as a great body like an immense bird sails overhead, casting a grotesque shadow. An elderly man on a porch starts up in alarm. Contents promise twenty-five chapters, beginning with news of a treasure wreck and finishing the submarine.

Mr. Berg is astonished and suspicious, Tom is imprisoned, and tables turn before a trial dive. Later headings bring the ocean bed, diving suits, a tropical island race, sharks, and ramming the wreck. Readers get an underwater treasure adventure where the new boat is tested against rivals and the sea.
